questions.q: What is the core analogy the lesson uses to describe what an Operational Readiness Review does for a service before launch?
options: It functions like a marketing launch checklist with no technical content
It functions like a performance review for the team, not the service
It functions like a legal contract sign-off unrelated to the service's behavior
It functions like code review: a second set of eyes catches problems before they merge into production
questions.explain: An ORR applies the same principle as code review to operations: before real traffic hits a service, someone outside the building team confirms the operational basics are genuinely in place.

questions.q: Which five areas does a real ORR checklist cover, according to this lesson?
options: Monitoring, alerting, runbooks, capacity, and rollback plan
Branding, pricing, marketing copy, legal terms, and support staffing
Code style, test coverage percentage, linter rules, git history, and commit message format
Office location, team headcount, budget, vendor contracts, and org chart
questions.explain: The five areas are monitoring (dashboards and defined SLIs/SLOs), alerting (routed and tied to runbooks), runbooks (tested, not just written), capacity (load-tested with dependency checks), and a tested rollback plan.

questions.q: Why does the lesson say an alert passing an ORR checklist needs to be tied to a runbook and checked for noise, not just confirmed to exist?
options: Because alerts without runbooks are automatically disabled by most paging tools
Because an alert that fires on normal, expected behavior gets ignored by the time a real incident needs it
Because ORRs are only concerned with alert volume, never alert accuracy
Because runbooks are optional once a service reaches its first follow-up review
questions.explain: An alert that pages on noise erodes trust and gets ignored, so a real ORR checks both that each alert routes correctly and that it's been confirmed not to fire on normal behavior.

questions.q: Why does the lesson recommend that ORR sign-off authority sit with someone outside the team that built the service?
options: Outside reviewers are legally required for all production launches
The building team's own blind spots mean they may not notice gaps in what they didn't think to test, similar to why code review isn't self-approved
Only external consultants are allowed to approve a go-live
It has no real effect; sign-off location is purely procedural
questions.explain: A team confident about what it tested may not notice what it didn't test; sign-off from an SRE lead, platform representative, or rotating peer mirrors why a pull request isn't approved by its own author.

questions.q: What is the purpose of the post-launch follow-up review, typically held two to four weeks after go-live?
options: To replace the pre-launch ORR checklist entirely going forward
To re-assign the service to a different on-call team
To validate the pre-launch ORR's assumptions against real production data, catching things like noisier-than-expected alerts or SLO drift under real traffic
To cancel the service if it has had zero incidents since launch
questions.explain: A pre-launch ORR can't catch everything that only shows up under real production load; the follow-up review checks the service against actual production data to close that loop.
